intro: Wagner’s overture to Tannhäuser, WWV 70, in Sousa’s arrangement for concert band, played by the United States Marine Band. The pilgrims’ hymn leads into the music of Venus’s mountain and then returns with the quick figures still around it, and the clarinets take over the strings’ fast lines.

sections.label: A · Pilgrims’ hymn, B♭ major
sections.mNote: Clarinet, bassoon and horns begin the hymn quietly in B♭ major.

sections.label: A′ · Hymn in brass
sections.mNote: Broad brass phrases over running figures in the first clarinets

sections.label: B · Venus’s mountain music, quick clarinet figures
sections.mNote: Quick clarinet figures pass to the upper woodwind.

sections.label: C · Solo clarinet with upper woodwind
sections.mNote: A solo clarinet plays over figures in the upper woodwind.

sections.label: B′ · Song to Venus, B♭, return
sections.mNote: The song returns in B♭ over moving lower parts.

sections.label: A′ · Pilgrims’ hymn under running clarinets
sections.mNote: The hymn returns under continuous running figures in the first clarinets.

sections.label: A″ · Closing hymn, B♭ major, full band
sections.mNote: Full brass and upper winds play the closing B♭-major hymn.

relations.label: The Venus song returns higher
relations.basis: The broad song in the fast Venusberg section is restated in the renewed fast span. The five-semitone upward pitch-class shift is consistent with its move to another tonal level; the listening notes distinguish this song from the pilgrims’ hymn. CENS diagonal mean 0.940, sustained 34.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift +5 semitones and time offset 174 s (cache/form/wagner-tannhauser-overture.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The pilgrims’ hymn returns
relations.basis: The overture’s closing frame restores the pilgrims’ hymn after the Venusberg music. The earlier excerpt comes from the hymn’s first broad statement, while the later one follows the return marked near 665 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.934, sustained 14 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 527 s (cache/form/wagner-tannhauser-overture.txt, candidate 5; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Pilgrims’ hymn, opening statement
cues.text: The hymn begins quietly in clarinet, bassoon and horns. In the opera, its long B♭-major phrases belong to the pilgrims travelling to Rome. Sousa keeps the scoring spare, and the band’s brightest instruments rest.
cues.evidence: John Philip Sousa’s band transcription, printed p. 1, Andante maestoso: solo B♭ clarinet, bassoons, horns, lower clarinets and bass. https://www.marineband.marines.mil/Portals/175/Docs/Sheet%20Music/Tannhauser/tannhauser_score.pdf?ver=2018-10-17-112418-240. Dramatic identification: Marc Mandel, Boston Symphony programme note, https://www.bso.org/works/overture-and-venusberg-music-from-tannh%C3%A4user.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hymn in the brass, clarinet semiquavers
cues.text: The brass play the hymn in broad, even notes. Above them the first clarinets play continuous semiquavers in 3/4, taking the part Wagner wrote for the orchestral strings.
cues.evidence: Sousa band score, opening full hymn, including printed pp. 10–12: brass melody and first-clarinet semiquavers in 3/4.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The song contest at the Wartburg
cues.text: Tannhäuser leaves Venus’s realm, then sings her praises at the Wartburg song contest. The other singers turn on him. Elisabeth protects him, and he joins the pilgrims bound for Rome.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel, Boston Symphony programme note, plot synopsis and account of the overture: https://www.bso.org/works/overture-and-venusberg-music-from-tannh%C3%A4user.

cues.title: Venusberg music, Allegro
cues.text: From bar 82, Venus’s music begins with short running figures in the clarinets, followed by the upper woodwind at pp. The bass and heavy brass stop. Wagner changes the hymn’s three-beat metre to common time and marks the passage Allegro.
cues.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 19–20, bar 82 onwards: Allegro, change from 3/4 to common time, lower-clarinet figures and pp upper-wind answers.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Solo clarinet, rehearsal D
cues.text: At rehearsal D the solo clarinet plays a long melody. Flute, piccolo and E♭ clarinet play running figures around it. The bass and brass have extended rests.
cues.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 39–42, quieter episode at rehearsal D: solo clarinet and upper-wind figures, with extended rests in bass and brass.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the hymn to Venus
cues.text: The broad melody of Tannhäuser’s hymn to Venus returns in B♭ major. Beneath it, the lower clarinets, saxophones and euphonium play continuous flowing lines.
cues.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 49–50, rehearsal E, Tempo I and B♭-major restatement. Mandel identifies the central broad melody as Tannhäuser’s hymn to Venus.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Paris production, 1861
cues.text: For the Paris production of 1861, Wagner placed the ballet in Act I. Members of the Jockey Club wanted the dancing later in the evening, and their whistles and catcalls disrupted the performances. Wagner withdrew the opera after three nights.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel, Boston Symphony programme note, account of the Paris production, first-act ballet, Jockey Club disruption and withdrawal after three performances.

cues.title: Return of the hymn
cues.text: The hymn returns in the middle and lower wind parts. Above it the first clarinets continue their semiquavers. Wagner brings back the procession and keeps the mountain music going at the same time.
cues.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 62–66, returning hymn and continuing first-clarinet semiquavers.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cosima Wagner’s diary, 1883
cues.text: On 23 January 1883 Cosima wrote in her diary: “He says he still owes the world Tannhäuser.” Wagner had then spent nearly forty years returning to the opera.
cues.evidence: Cosima Wagner’s diary, 23 January 1883, quoted in Marc Mandel’s Boston Symphony programme note: https://www.bso.org/works/overture-and-venusberg-music-from-tannh%C3%A4user.

cues.title: Hymn in B♭ major, full band
cues.text: The upper winds and full brass play the hymn in B♭ major. Under it the clarinets continue their quick figures. Sousa scores the long melody for the whole band.
cues.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 76–79, rehearsal H, Assai stretto: expanded wind and brass doublings over continuous first clarinets.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Brass take the hymn melody
transitions.how: The hymn stays in B♭ major and in 3/4. The brass play its long notes, and the first clarinets take a continuous semiquaver part above them. The low instruments mark out the bass beneath the two layers.
transitions.evidence: Sousa band score, opening build and full hymn, including printed pp. 10–12: B♭ major, 3/4, brass melody, first-clarinet semiquavers.

transitions.title: From the hymn to the Allegro
transitions.to: B · Venus’s mountain music, quick clarinet figures
transitions.how: The B♭-major hymn thins out to sustained wind notes. At the Allegro (bar 82), the metre changes from 3/4 to common time and the lower clarinets begin a soft rising figure. Flute, oboe and upper clarinets follow at pp with chromatic turns. The bass instruments rest.
transitions.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 19–20, bar 82 and following: Allegro, common time, clarinet figures, upper-wind pp entries, bass rests.

transitions.title: Solo clarinet over quiet wind figures
transitions.from: B · Venus’s mountain music, quick clarinet figures
transitions.to: C · Solo clarinet with upper woodwind
transitions.how: The loud chords stop, and quiet falling and rising figures follow in the wind. The low bass drops out. The solo clarinet plays a sustained line, with smaller notes in the flute, piccolo and E♭ clarinet around it. At Un poco ritenuto the phrase slows for a moment and the melody is held above the accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 39–42, approach to rehearsal D and the clarinet episode.

transitions.title: F-major dominant preparation for B♭ at Tempo I
transitions.from: C · Solo clarinet with upper woodwind
transitions.to: B′ · Song to Venus, B♭, return
transitions.how: The band holds F-major harmony, then repeats it in short, accented chords. F is the dominant of B♭. At Tempo I, rehearsal E, the Venus song returns in B♭ major. The lower clarinets, saxophones and euphonium play flowing quavers beneath the broader upper melody.
transitions.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 49–50, sustained dominant preparation and rehearsal E, Tempo I.

transitions.title: The hymn returns under running clarinets
transitions.from: B′ · Song to Venus, B♭, return
transitions.to: A′ · Pilgrims’ hymn under running clarinets
transitions.how: The fast music thins out towards B♭ major. The hymn returns in the lower clarinets, horns and saxophones over long sustained bass notes. Above it the first clarinets continue their semiquavers.
transitions.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 62–66: returning hymn in the middle and low winds, running first clarinets and sustained bass support.

transitions.title: Full band takes up the hymn
transitions.from: A′ · Pilgrims’ hymn under running clarinets
transitions.to: A″ · Closing hymn, B♭ major, full band
transitions.how: At rehearsal H, marked Assai stretto, the upper winds and full brass join the B♭-major hymn. The bass doubles its steps and the first clarinets continue their running figures. Long notes spread from the low brass to the top of the wind section, and the running accompaniment continues within them.
transitions.evidence: Sousa band score, printed pp. 76–79: rehearsal H, Assai stretto, enlarged wind and brass doublings and continuing first-clarinet figures.

source.title: Wagner, Tannhäuser Overture, concert-band full score, arranged by John Philip Sousa
source.locator: Printed pp. 1–91; opening, A, Allegro, D, E, returning chorale and H. Alto clarinet is grouped with clarinets, and flugelhorns with cornets. Passage timings are approximate.

timeline.note: Bassoons, solo clarinet and horns share the hymn above alto clarinet, bass clarinet and tuba.
Oboe and euphonium broaden the melodic line; saxophones and low reeds thicken its support.
The brass play the hymn while the first clarinets play the rapid figures above it.
Quiet clarinet runs begin the fast music. The upper woodwinds answer above lighter support in the lower winds.
The Venus song is expanded and played by the whole orchestra over running woodwind figures, with fuller support from the brass.
Solo clarinet holds the line against figures in the flute, piccolo and E♭ clarinet. The heavy brass stop.
The Venus song returns with full-band doublings above moving saxophones, low clarinets and euphoniums.
Lower winds and horns bring back the hymn beneath the first clarinets’ continuing rapid line.
The upper woodwinds double the brass hymn, and the clarinets continue their figuration around its long notes.
Running figures lead into the band’s sustained final chords and a close supported by the timpani.

composer.epithet: Composer who placed the orchestra beneath the stage at Bayreuth, hidden from the audience.
facts: Theodor Weinlig, Leipzig, 1831; then the daily work of provincial opera houses
Dresden court conductor, 1843–49 · Bayreuth Festival founder, 1876
Wrote his own librettos; published essays on theatre, music and politics
Thirteen completed operas, including the four evenings of the Ring
composer.background:
In 1839 Richard Wagner and his wife Minna fled Riga ahead of their creditors and took a storm-battered ship to London. He was twenty-six, an opera conductor with two completed operas and no real success. The sea passage stayed with him. A story by Heinrich Heine about a captain condemned to sail for ever became Der fliegende Holländer; its overture begins over a bare fifth, with horns and bassoons playing against the storm music in the strings. The Wagners went on to Paris, where he made arrangements for publishers and tried to get his music staged.

He grew up in the theatre. Born in Leipzig in 1813, he lost his father as an infant and moved with his mother into the household of Ludwig Geyer, an actor and painter in Dresden. Wagner wanted to write plays before he knew how to write music. He heard Weber’s Der Freischütz and Beethoven’s symphonies, and in 1831 he took counterpoint lessons from Theodor Weinlig. Posts followed in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga. Die Feen was not performed, and Das Liebesverbot, his operatic version of Measure for Measure, failed after one performance in 1836. That year he married Minna, an actress.
